# AI in the interface

How AI behaves inside the product: where it's offered, how its suggestions are accepted and undone, how its output is marked and sourced, how sure it says it is, how it acts on someone's behalf, how it waits, fails, learns, remembers, listens and sees, and how it hands over. The aim throughout is the right amount of reliance, not the most trust.

Not covered here: where AI surfaces sit on a screen, how the composer is built, AI wording, and the look of the AI mark.

**When principles conflict.** Accessibility minimums come first. A product's own shell and established patterns come next, and win over the defaults here. A more specific principle wins over a general one. Where two files disagree, the one whose subject it is wins.

**Terms used here**
- **Assistant, composer, AI mark:** the assistant is the product's conversational AI surface; the composer is its input, with context, scope, controls and submit; the AI mark is the label, in words as well as any icon or colour, that marks something as AI-produced.
- **Compact, medium, expanded:** window widths. Compact is phones and rugged handhelds in portrait, medium is small tablets and handhelds in landscape, and expanded is large tablets and desktop. Layout follows width, never the type of device.
- **Shared device:** one device used by several people in turn, who sign in at the device.

---

## 1. Where AI is offered
9.1. **The size of the job decides where AI appears:**
    - On one item or field: an entry point on that item, taking no permanent space.
    - Help while working in a screen: a side panel beside the work, which leaves the work visible.
    - Work across the whole product: the full assistant.

    A screen may combine the first with either of the others.
9.2. **AI is offered where the work already is:** a suggestion at the field, a summary at the top of what it summarises, an action in the toolbar. It opens the assistant only when the person chooses to continue in conversation.
9.3. **An AI action on a screen is an ordinary action with the AI mark.** It follows the same rules as any other action, and is secondary unless it's the screen's main purpose. Its label names the action ("Summarise"), and the mark carries the "AI". It sits with the non-AI actions that do the same kind of job.
9.4. **A writing aid in a field appears when the field has focus,** and only on fields where it genuinely helps.
9.5. **An AI feature is introduced when it first becomes relevant,** in context rather than in a tour.
9.6. **Proactive offers follow the state of the content.** Nothing is offered that can't apply: no "Summarise" on an empty page. Only a few likely-useful offers are shown at once, and by default an offer waits until the task's main step is done. It interrupts mid-task only to prevent an error.
9.7. **By default, a product has one assistant entry point.** Specialised agents are reached through it and named by their job. It says what it is, keeps one position, stays reachable on every screen where tasks span screens, and states its scope in one line suited to the current screen.
9.8. **Every AI entry point is recognisable as AI.** Output the AI generated, chose or ranked for the person is marked. Long-established recognition, such as barcode decoding, spell check or speech-to-text, isn't.
9.9. **Every task the person is accountable for can be finished without AI.** Conveniences that only AI provides (a summary, natural-language search) say when they're unavailable. AI entry points stay visible and say why.

## 2. Suggestions and AI-filled values
9.10. **A suggestion is shown as a proposal before it takes effect,** next to what it would change and kept apart from it. Nothing written by a person is overwritten without their say.
9.11. **Accept, reject and refine sit on the suggestion itself.** Rejecting is as easy as accepting.
9.12. **An accepted suggestion applies in place, and can be undone right there.** The product acknowledges that it took effect.
9.13. **An AI-filled value stays marked until a person accepts or edits it.** Once edited, the mark becomes a way back to the AI value.
9.14. **A value the AI chose for the person (an owner, a category, a priority) shows its reason beside it.**
9.15. **Correcting AI is fine-grained:** switch a category, edit part of the text, undo one automated action, or correct many items at once. A correction takes effect at once, is remembered by default (subject to 9.58 and the tenant's policy), and can itself be corrected.
9.16. **When there are several options, they're kept few and different from each other, with the most likely first.**
9.17. **By default, an AI fill across many records is checked on a few first.** The person reviews those before the rest are filled. Low-risk fills that are easy to undo may skip the sample.
9.18. **By default, each AI action on a field creates a version.** A single fill that undo already covers (9.12) needs none. The person can step between versions, and the version controls appear only once there's more than one. Regenerating adds a new version beside the last, never silently replacing it.

## 3. Marking and sources
9.19. **AI output is marked wherever it appears, at the smallest unit that holds all of it.** A field, a message, a card or a section each carries its own mark. Where a whole collection or column is AI-produced, it's marked once at its heading, not on every cell.
9.20. **The mark names what the AI did** ("Summarised", "Drafted", "Ranked by"), so the person knows what to check.
9.21. **The mark opens a layered explanation:** first what the AI did and why in a few short sentences, then the supporting details, sources and data used. The deepest layer is always reachable for high-stakes output.
9.22. **AI marks stay on earlier messages after a person joins a conversation,** so it's always clear who said what.
9.23. **Sources sit next to the claim they support,** labelled by what they are, not "Source". Each one previews in place and opens at the exact passage where the source allows it.
9.24. **A missing or broken source is shown as missing, never filled in.**
9.25. **Sources are never presented as proof.** On high-stakes output, they come with a prompt to check them.
9.26. **AI content copied, exported or sent before a person has taken it over carries its mark and source.** Once a person has edited and owned it, the content travels as theirs, and the record (9.41) keeps its AI origin.
9.27. **An AI value on a scale (risk, priority, likelihood) carries its key and when it was worked out.**

## 4. Confidence and checking what was meant
9.28. **Confidence is shown only where it's known to match how often the AI is right, and only where it changes what the person does.** Otherwise it isn't shown.
9.29. **Confidence is said in words, each tied to what to do. Numbers are usually shown only to people whose role uses them, and only ever when calibrated.** A ranked order can carry confidence on its own: the most likely comes first.
9.30. **How sure the AI is changes what it does:**
    - Sure: it answers, or proposes the action.
    - Less sure: it offers a few alternatives, most likely first, for the person to choose.
    - Not sure enough: it says so, explains why, and offers a way forward.

    Confidence decides whether it answers, offers alternatives or asks. Harm and reversibility decide whether it confirms first (9.35).
9.31. **The doubtful parts are marked, not just the whole answer.**
9.32. **When the AI isn't sure what the person meant, it asks by default.** Where asking costs more than a narrow action would (hands busy, low risk, easily undone), it takes the narrower, safer reading and says which one it took.
9.33. **A clarifying question asks only about the doubtful detail ("Bin A-14 or A-41?"), and only when the answer will be used.** A question card waits for the answer; it never times out into a guess.

## 5. Acting on someone's behalf
9.34. **Work in the confirm-first tier (9.35) is shown in full before it runs, with Confirm and Cancel.** The preview shows the thing itself: the message, the order, the setting.
9.35. **The weight of a confirmation follows harm, reach and reversibility.** Low-risk work such as searching or drafting runs without asking. Easily undone work is checked afterwards. Anything that costs money, reaches other people, affects safety or can't be undone is confirmed first. Asking about routine work wears confirmation out.
9.36. **A confirmation is readable in the time it's given.** It shows what's needed to judge it. A confirmation people can only click through doesn't count.
9.37. **By default, work with several steps shows its plan first,** as a short list the person can approve, edit one step of, or stop. Cost, reach and permissions needed are shown with it. Low-risk, read-only multi-step work may just show its progress.
9.38. **While the work runs, the plan becomes its progress.** Each step shows as waiting, running, needing approval, failed, retried or done. A change from the plan is shown, explained and confirmed again.
9.39. **Stop is always in the same place, and takes effect at the next safe point.** Steps that can't be interrupted, such as writing firmware, say so before they start. It shows what stopped, what had already been done, and what happens to the finished parts.
9.40. **Long work runs in the background,** and the person is told where they are when it finishes or needs them.
9.41. **Automated actions can be undone where possible,** and leave a record: what was done, when, on whose approval, from what data.
9.42. **Where a person's approval is required, the approve and reject actions sit on the item that needs them,** and the item names who else must approve, if anyone.
9.43. **When checking is switched off for a kind of action, that's shown clearly, and can be switched back on at any time.**

## 6. Waiting and streaming
9.44. **AI work shows that it's running at once,** in the place its result will appear. The result never moves the person away from where they were.
9.45. **Progress says what's being done ("Checking 12 devices"),** never filler, and changes to the past tense when finished.
9.46. **Output streams in as it's produced. The view stays at the start of the new output and doesn't chase the end.**
9.47. **The control that started the work becomes Stop, in the same place.** By default, stopping in a field restores what was there before, unless the person chooses to keep the partial text. When the work finishes, the control offers to refine or regenerate.
9.48. **Reasoning is shown as steps and sources, not as a running inner monologue.** For multi-step work, the plan and its progress are the visible trace (9.38). It sits in a bounded, collapsible area, and each result links to the step that produced it.

## 7. Failures and limits
9.50. **An AI failure says what failed and why, in plain words, and gives a next step.** It uses the product's normal message patterns.
9.51. **A request the AI won't or can't handle is acknowledged and redirected** to what it can do, with an example that would work. It never ends at "I can't help with that".
9.52. **A failure never ends in a vague promise.** It points to another way to finish the task, including doing it without AI.
9.53. **A limit (usage, time, permission) is stated before it's reached where possible.** When it's reached, the limit says what's affected and what the person can do now.
9.54. **AI that needs a connection says so while offline, at the feature.** Queued work is held, not run blind. When the connection returns, it's checked against the current state and confirmed again if anything changed. Work that can't wait is done another way.
9.55. **After repeated failures or rejections, the AI asks what's wrong, or offers a person.**

## 8. Feedback and learning
9.56. **Feedback is always voluntary and quick. By default, each AI answer carries a positive and a negative.** Voice and wearables skip it, and inline suggestions count accepting or rejecting as feedback. It's shown on the latest answer, and on focus or hover for earlier ones. A negative may open a short set of reasons in plain words.
9.57. **Acknowledging feedback says what happens to it.** It promises a change only when one is scheduled.
9.58. **Learning from what people do is disclosed. Opting out is offered at the level that decides it: the person, or the tenant, in which case the product says so.** The AI adapts gradually, and says when its behaviour has changed.

## 9. Memory, consent and privacy
9.59. **What the AI remembers is shown when it's saved, and can be seen, edited and deleted in one place.** Resetting to no memory is one step. Audit records, and anything the tenant must keep, are separate from memory and say so.
9.60. **Memory has a scope:** the person, the task or project, or this session only. It never carries personal details into unrelated work.
9.61. **On a shared device, memory belongs to the person, not the device.** When the person changes, their conversations, suggestions and memory leave the screen.
9.62. **Capture is disclosed before it starts. Where the person's own consent is the basis, it's asked separately for recording, for training and for sharing.** In a workplace, the tenant often authorises capture instead, and the disclosure says who did. Declining training never disables the product. Consent can be withdrawn at any time, with a statement of what will be deleted and when.
9.63. **A visible indicator shows whenever the AI is listening, recording or watching.** On a device without a screen, that's a light, sound or vibration.
9.64. **A private mode is unmistakable on every screen while it's on,** with one fixed line saying what it means.
9.65. **The product says when data leaves the device.** It never infers personal traits; it asks.

## 10. Voice
9.66. **Spoken replies are short, one or two sentences a turn, and make sense without the screen.** They assume they may be overheard.
9.67. **Spoken replies also show as text wherever there's a screen.** Without one, the last reply can be replayed. On a device without a history, the last line shows once as a caption.
9.68. **By default, what the person said is shown as text before it's acted on, so it can be corrected.** Read-only requests run at once, with what was heard echoed. In push-to-talk, releasing sends it, with the text shown and a brief chance to cancel. Hands-busy and in-vehicle use read the text back aloud instead of asking for a look.
9.69. **When the AI didn't understand, it asks again about only the missing part, then offers examples.** After about two misses it hands over to the screen or to a person. When nothing was heard, it rephrases rather than saying it heard nothing.
9.70. **Voice never blocks the person's hearing of their surroundings,** and a false start is easy to dismiss.

## 11. Camera and scanning
9.71. **The camera view keeps its centre clear.** Controls sit at the top and bottom edges.
9.72. **A frame or marker shows what the camera is doing:** looking, too far away, checking, or failed. Short guidance states the condition ("Move closer"), not a command to tap.
9.73. **For visual recognition, the view freezes on a detection and gives the person a moment to cancel before anything is looked up.** Barcode scanning keeps the device's own continuous behaviour.
9.74. **Results appear in a sheet over the captured image, most likely first, with the captured image for comparison.** Markers on the image show where each result sits. In a form, the result returns to the field that asked for it.
9.75. **No result, or low confidence, shows a message with help (angle, distance, light) and a way to try again,** plus typing as the alternative.

## 12. Summaries in screens
9.76. **A summary states what it covers** (this device, this shift, this site), is marked as AI, and links each point to its source.
9.77. **A summary can be shortened, expanded or switched off,** and stays faithful rather than brief where the source matters (agreements, safety).
9.78. **A summary shows when it was made, and says when the data behind it has changed since.**
9.79. **A reason given for a ranking or recommendation states facts** ("Because this bin was short twice this week"), never feelings about the person.
9.80. **An AI notice sits with the AI region it describes, never in a page footer.**

## 13. Handing over
9.81. **A request for a person is acted on at once:** connected, queued with a real wait, or told when someone is next available. A person is also offered after repeated failure or frustration.
9.82. **Before a conversation starts, the product says the AI answers first and a person follows if needed,** and when people are available.
9.83. **Waiting for a person shows a real time estimate by default, and the queue position when no estimate is reliable.** Everything said so far goes with the hand-over, so nobody starts again.
9.84. **Work handed to another product says so in both places, in the past tense** ("Draft created in the work order app"), with one action to open it.

## 14. Reliance
9.85. **Where a wrong answer could harm someone, the AI says why as well as what,** and shows the data it used. The product doesn't use generated content where a mistake would cause real harm without a person checking.
9.86. **The moment a person takes ownership of AI output (saves, sends, shares, inserts it) is where a check sits on high-stakes work.** It says they're taking ownership.
9.87. **Checking is made easy rather than urged:** doubtful parts marked (9.31), sources in place (9.23), the case for and against where it matters, and long output produced in reviewable parts.
9.88. **The AI never presents itself as a person.** It has no feelings, isn't called a team member, and uses "I" only about its own work.

## 15. Work, fleets and authority
9.89. **AI never makes the final decision on a person's schedule, tasks, workload or performance.** A manager approves it, and the worker affected can see the reason, stated as work facts, and contest it.
9.90. **A queue of AI drafts for approval leads with what changed since the last approved version, and with any item that breaks a rule.** Clean items can be approved together. Flagged items are approved one at a time.
9.91. **An AI change aimed at many devices or printers shows how many and which, runs on a small group first, and offers a rollback before reaching the rest.**
9.92. **The AI acts only with the person's own permissions, inside the current tenant and site.** It never draws on another tenant's data, and every bulk action shows its scope.
9.93. **An action the AI proposes because of something it read (a log, an email, a document) shows where the idea came from, and is always confirmed.** Text inside content is never treated as the person's request.
9.94. **Safety steps, standard procedures and compliance wording are quoted from the approved source and linked.** They're never paraphrased or generated.
9.95. **Before an approved action runs, it's checked against the current state.** If the device, stock or schedule has changed since approval, the person sees the difference and confirms again.
9.96. **While a vehicle is moving, AI replies are spoken and need no reading.** Anything that needs the screen waits until the vehicle stops.
9.97. **An AI exchange cut off by a scan, a call, docking or sign-out resumes where it stopped, for the same person only (9.61).** A pending confirmation never runs while the person is away.
9.98. **Alerts the AI raises are ranked by consequence, grouped by cause, and each says why it was raised.** Dismissing one with a reason tunes the ones that follow.
9.99. **The AI replies in the person's interface language, whatever language its sources are in.** A translated source is marked as translated. Voice listens for the person's set language.
9.100. **People who receive something the AI sent or changed can see that the AI did it, for which role, and who approved it.**
